Tomato___Early_blight.description: Dark concentric-ringed spots on older leaves, often with yellow halos, progressing upward and causing defoliation.
Tomato___Early_blight.organic_treatment: Spray neem oil (5ml/L) or copper-based fungicide every 7-10 days; remove and destroy infected leaves.
Tomato___Early_blight.chemical_treatment: Apply Mancozeb 75% WP or Chlorothalonil at first symptom onset, repeat every 10-14 days.
Tomato___Early_blight.dosage_guidance: Mancozeb: 2-2.5 g/L water; Chlorothalonil: 2 g/L water. General guidance only — always confirm against the product label for your region.
Tomato___Early_blight.recovery_recommendations: Remove and destroy affected lower leaves, improve airflow by pruning, and resume normal watering once new growth appears healthy.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Water-soaked pale-green to brown lesions on leaves that rapidly enlarge, with white fungal growth on the underside in humid conditions; can destroy a crop within days.
Tomato___Late_blight.organic_treatment: Copper-based fungicide sprays every 5-7 days during humid weather; remove infected plants immediately to prevent spread.
Tomato___Late_blight.chemical_treatment: Apply a systemic fungicide such as Metalaxyl + Mancozeb at first sign of disease; repeat every 7 days in favorable (cool, wet) weather.
Tomato___Late_blight.dosage_guidance: Metalaxyl+Mancozeb: 2.5 g/L water. Spray thoroughly covering both leaf surfaces. General guidance only.
Tomato___Late_blight.recovery_recommendations: This disease spreads extremely fast in cool wet weather — remove and burn/bury infected plants immediately rather than waiting for recovery, to protect the rest of the field.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit that later turn scabby; leaves may yellow and drop.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment: Copper-based bactericide sprays every 7 days; avoid working in wet fields to reduce spread.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment: Copper hydroxide combined with Mancozeb improves control; streptomycin-based sprays where locally approved.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.dosage_guidance: Copper hydroxide: 2-3 g/L water, every 7-10 days. Bacterial diseases do not respond to fungicides alone.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.recovery_recommendations: Remove severely infected leaves, avoid handling wet foliage, and improve field drainage to reduce bacterial spread.

Tomato___Leaf_curl_virus.causal_agent: Tomato leaf curl virus (Begomovirus), transmitted by whitefly
Tomato___Leaf_curl_virus.description: Upward curling and crinkling of leaves, stunted plant growth, yellowing leaf margins, and reduced fruit set.
Tomato___Leaf_curl_virus.organic_treatment: No cure exists once infected — focus on controlling the whitefly vector with yellow sticky traps and neem oil sprays.
Tomato___Leaf_curl_virus.chemical_treatment: Control whitefly vector with systemic insecticides such as Imidacloprid or Thiamethoxam; remove and destroy infected plants.
Tomato___Leaf_curl_virus.dosage_guidance: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL: 0.3-0.5 ml/L water as a foliar spray targeting whitefly. Viral infection itself cannot be treated chemically.
Tomato___Leaf_curl_virus.recovery_recommendations: Infected plants do not recover — rogue out (remove) infected plants promptly to protect the rest of the field and focus on vector control.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Target-shaped brown spots with concentric rings, mainly on older leaves, leading to leaf yellowing and drop.
Potato___Early_blight.organic_treatment: Neem oil or copper fungicide sprays every 7-10 days; remove infected foliage.
Potato___Early_blight.chemical_treatment: Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil at 10-14 day intervals starting at first symptom.
Potato___Early_blight.dosage_guidance: Mancozeb: 2-2.5 g/L water, repeat every 10-14 days. General guidance only.
prevention_tips: Maintain plant vigor with adequate potassium
Potato___Early_blight.recovery_recommendations: Remove lower infected leaves and maintain balanced fertilization; new growth should be symptom-free once fungicide program is followed.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn brown/black, with white mold on undersides in humid conditions; can also rot tubers in storage.
Potato___Late_blight.organic_treatment: Copper-based fungicide every 5-7 days during cool, wet weather; destroy infected plants and volunteer tubers.
Potato___Late_blight.chemical_treatment: Metalaxyl + Mancozeb or Cymoxanil-based systemic fungicides at first symptom, repeat every 7 days in favorable weather.
Potato___Late_blight.dosage_guidance: Metalaxyl+Mancozeb: 2.5 g/L water. General guidance only — confirm against local product label.
prevention_tips: Avoid irrigation late in the day
Potato___Late_blight.recovery_recommendations: Destroy severely infected plants immediately; this disease spreads too fast to wait for natural recovery.

Corn___Common_rust.description: Small, reddish-brown, powdery pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces that release rust-colored spores when touched.
Corn___Common_rust.organic_treatment: Generally minor — sulfur-based fungicide sprays if severe; ensure good plant nutrition to build tolerance.
Corn___Common_rust.chemical_treatment: Propiconazole or Azoxystrobin-based fungicides if infection is heavy and plants are young.
Corn___Common_rust.dosage_guidance: Propiconazole: 1 ml/L water. Usually only needed for severe infections on susceptible hybrids.
Corn___Common_rust.recovery_recommendations: Mature plants usually outgrow mild rust without intervention; focus fungicide use only on young, heavily infected plantings.

Corn___Gray_leaf_spot.description: Rectangular, tan-to-gray lesions running parallel to leaf veins, which can merge and blight large areas of the leaf.
Corn___Gray_leaf_spot.organic_treatment: Crop rotation and residue management are the primary organic controls; there is no strong organic fungicide alternative.
Corn___Gray_leaf_spot.chemical_treatment: Azoxystrobin or Pyraclostrobin-based fungicides applied at early tasseling if disease pressure is high.
Corn___Gray_leaf_spot.dosage_guidance: Azoxystrobin: 1 ml/L water, applied preventatively at early disease onset. General guidance only.
prevention_tips: Rotate away from corn for 1-2 years
Corn___Gray_leaf_spot.recovery_recommendations: Residue-borne disease — remove and till in crop debris after harvest to reduce spore carryover to next season.

Apple___Apple_scab.description: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit, which may crack and become corky as they mature.
Apple___Apple_scab.organic_treatment: Sulfur or copper-based fungicide sprays from bud break through petal fall; rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn.
Apple___Apple_scab.chemical_treatment: Captan or Myclobutanil-based fungicides applied on a 7-10 day schedule during wet spring weather.
Apple___Apple_scab.dosage_guidance: Captan: 2 g/L water, applied every 7-10 days during infection periods (wet spring weather).
prevention_tips: Rake and destroy fallen leaves each autumn
Apple___Apple_scab.recovery_recommendations: Existing scab lesions will not disappear, but new growth will be clean if the fungicide schedule is maintained through the wet season.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Small brown circular spots on leaves with dark borders; fruit develops brown spots that shrivel into hard black mummified berries.
Grape___Black_rot.organic_treatment: Remove mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning; sulfur-based sprays from bud break.
Grape___Black_rot.chemical_treatment: Mancozeb or Myclobutanil fungicide program from bud break through veraison, every 10-14 days.
Grape___Black_rot.dosage_guidance: Mancozeb: 2-2.5 g/L water. Critical spray windows are pre-bloom and immediately post-bloom.
prevention_tips: Remove mummified berries and infected wood each winter
Apply protective sprays before rain events
Grape___Black_rot.recovery_recommendations: Infected berries cannot recover; remove and destroy mummies to break the disease cycle for next season.

Pepper___Bacterial_spot.description: Small, water-soaked, dark lesions on leaves and fruit that may have a yellow halo; leaves can drop in severe cases.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment: Copper-based bactericide sprays every 7 days; avoid overhead watering and working wet plants.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment: Copper hydroxide combined with Mancozeb for improved efficacy; rotate copper sources to slow resistance.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.dosage_guidance: Copper hydroxide: 2-3 g/L water, every 7-10 days. Bacterial disease — fungicides alone will not control it.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.recovery_recommendations: Remove severely spotted leaves and fruit, and improve airflow; new growth should be cleaner once wet-weather spread is controlled.

Rice___Blast.description: Diamond-shaped lesions with gray centers and brown borders on leaves; can also infect the neck of the panicle, causing empty grains.
Rice___Blast.organic_treatment: Balanced nitrogen application (avoid excess) and resistant varieties are the main organic controls; silica-rich amendments can help.
Rice___Blast.chemical_treatment: Tricyclazole or Isoprothiolane-based fungicide at first symptom, with a second spray at panicle initiation if pressure continues.
Rice___Blast.dosage_guidance: Tricyclazole: 0.6 g/L water. Apply at first lesion sighting and again at booting/panicle stage in high-pressure seasons.
prevention_tips: Maintain adequate but not excess water
Rice___Blast.recovery_recommendations: Leaf blast lesions stop expanding once fungicide is applied; monitor closely at panicle stage since neck blast can cause irreversible yield loss.

Rice___Brown_spot.description: Oval brown spots with a gray-white center scattered across leaves; often linked to nutrient-poor soils.
Rice___Brown_spot.organic_treatment: Improve soil fertility (especially potassium and silicon); seed treatment with hot water or biocontrol agents.
Rice___Brown_spot.chemical_treatment: Mancozeb or Propiconazole-based fungicide sprays if severe.
Rice___Brown_spot.dosage_guidance: Mancozeb: 2 g/L water, 2 sprays 10 days apart. Often resolves once soil fertility (especially K) is corrected.
Rice___Brown_spot.recovery_recommendations: Correct underlying nutrient deficiency (commonly potassium) alongside fungicide use for lasting control.

Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.description: Water-soaked lesions starting at leaf tips/margins that turn yellow-white and dry out, sometimes wilting entire seedlings (kresek phase).
Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.organic_treatment: Balanced nitrogen (avoid excess), resistant varieties, and drainage management; copper sprays offer limited help.
Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.chemical_treatment: Copper oxychloride or Streptocycline-based sprays where locally approved; primarily managed through resistant varieties and field sanitation.
Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.dosage_guidance: Copper oxychloride: 2.5-3 g/L water. Bacterial disease — chemical options are limited; prevention is the main defense.
prevention_tips: Avoid clipping seedling leaf tips during transplanting
Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.recovery_recommendations: Drain and dry the field where possible, avoid further nitrogen top-dressing, and rely on resistant varieties in future plantings.

Cotton___Bacterial_blight.description: Angular water-soaked spots on leaves that turn black, and dark lesions on bolls that can cause premature boll drop.
Cotton___Bacterial_blight.organic_treatment: Copper-based bactericide sprays; use acid-delinted, disease-free seed.
Cotton___Bacterial_blight.chemical_treatment: Copper oxychloride combined with Streptocycline where approved, applied at first symptom.
Cotton___Bacterial_blight.dosage_guidance: Copper oxychloride: 2.5-3 g/L water, every 10 days during humid weather.
Cotton___Bacterial_blight.recovery_recommendations: Remove severely infected plant debris after harvest to reduce carryover; new flushes of growth are typically less affected once dry weather returns.

Cotton___Boll_rot.causal_agent: Complex of fungi (Fusarium, Aspergillus, Colletotrichum spp.)
Cotton___Boll_rot.description: Bolls develop water-soaked or brown decayed areas, often starting at the base, leading to premature opening and stained/reduced lint quality.
Cotton___Boll_rot.organic_treatment: Improve airflow through proper spacing and defoliation timing; avoid excess nitrogen which promotes dense canopy.
Cotton___Boll_rot.chemical_treatment: Copper oxychloride or Carbendazim-based sprays during boll development in humid conditions.
Cotton___Boll_rot.dosage_guidance: Carbendazim: 1 g/L water, applied at boll formation stage during wet weather.
prevention_tips: Avoid excess nitrogen and dense canopy
Control boll-damaging insects that create entry wounds
Cotton___Boll_rot.recovery_recommendations: Affected bolls will not recover; focus on protecting remaining healthy bolls and improving canopy airflow for the rest of the season.

Sugarcane___Red_rot.description: Reddish discoloration inside the cane with white cross-bands when split open; leaves show drying and reddening from the tip.
Sugarcane___Red_rot.organic_treatment: Use disease-free setts treated with hot water (50°C for 2 hours) before planting; avoid ratooning infected fields.
Sugarcane___Red_rot.chemical_treatment: Carbendazim seed-sett treatment before planting; no effective in-season chemical cure once established.
Sugarcane___Red_rot.dosage_guidance: Carbendazim sett dip: 1 g/L water for 10 minutes before planting. No effective spray exists once the cane is infected.
prevention_tips: Rotate out of sugarcane for a season if disease is severe
Sugarcane___Red_rot.recovery_recommendations: Once internal red rot is present, the cane cannot be cured — remove and destroy infected clumps and prevent planting infected setts in future seasons.

Banana___Sigatoka_leaf_spot.description: Pale yellow streaks on leaves that develop into brown-black elongated spots with yellow halos, reducing photosynthetic leaf area.
Banana___Sigatoka_leaf_spot.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy heavily spotted leaves regularly; improve plant spacing for airflow.
Banana___Sigatoka_leaf_spot.chemical_treatment: Propiconazole or Mancozeb-based fungicide sprays on a 2-3 week rotation during the rainy season.
Banana___Sigatoka_leaf_spot.dosage_guidance: Propiconazole: 1 ml/L water, every 2-3 weeks during humid/rainy periods.
prevention_tips: Remove and destroy infected leaves regularly (leaf sanitation)
Banana___Sigatoka_leaf_spot.recovery_recommendations: Regular leaf sanitation combined with the fungicide schedule allows new leaves to emerge clean within a few weeks.

Groundnut___Tikka_leaf_spot.description: Circular brown to black spots on leaflets, often with a yellow halo, causing premature leaf drop and reduced pod fill.
Groundnut___Tikka_leaf_spot.organic_treatment: Neem-based sprays and crop rotation; remove and destroy crop debris after harvest.
Groundnut___Tikka_leaf_spot.chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb-based fungicide sprays starting 30-35 days after sowing, repeated every 10-15 days.
Groundnut___Tikka_leaf_spot.dosage_guidance: Chlorothalonil: 2 g/L water, every 10-15 days starting a month after sowing.
Groundnut___Tikka_leaf_spot.recovery_recommendations: Timely fungicide sprays before pod-fill stage protect yield even if some lower leaves are already affected.

Chilli___Anthracnose_fruit_rot.description: Sunken, dark, circular spots on ripening fruit with concentric rings of pink/orange spore masses in humid conditions.
Chilli___Anthracnose_fruit_rot.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy infected fruit; copper-based fungicide sprays during fruit development.
Chilli___Anthracnose_fruit_rot.chemical_treatment: Carbendazim or Mancozeb-based sprays starting at fruit set, every 10 days in humid weather.
Chilli___Anthracnose_fruit_rot.dosage_guidance: Carbendazim: 1 g/L water, every 10 days from fruit set through harvest in humid conditions.
prevention_tips: Remove and destroy infected fruit immediately
Chilli___Anthracnose_fruit_rot.recovery_recommendations: Infected fruit should be removed and destroyed; remaining healthy fruit can be protected with a consistent fungicide schedule.

Onion___Purple_blotch.description: Small white flecks that enlarge into purple-brown concentric-ringed lesions on leaves and seed stalks, often starting at older leaf tips.
Onion___Purple_blotch.organic_treatment: Neem oil sprays and balanced fertilization; avoid waterlogging.
Onion___Purple_blotch.chemical_treatment: Mancozeb or Iprodione-based fungicide sprays every 7-10 days during humid weather.
Onion___Purple_blotch.dosage_guidance: Mancozeb: 2-2.5 g/L water, every 7-10 days in humid conditions.
Onion___Purple_blotch.recovery_recommendations: New leaf growth is typically unaffected once humidity drops and the fungicide program is followed.

Mango___Anthracnose.description: Dark, sunken spots on leaves, flowers, and fruit; can cause flower/fruit drop and post-harvest fruit rot.
Mango___Anthracnose.organic_treatment: Copper-based sprays during flowering and fruit development; hot water treatment of harvested fruit (52°C, 5 minutes).
Mango___Anthracnose.chemical_treatment: Carbendazim or Mancozeb-based sprays at flowering, and again at pea-sized fruit stage.
Mango___Anthracnose.dosage_guidance: Carbendazim: 1 g/L water, at flowering and again at fruit-set stage.
Mango___Anthracnose.recovery_recommendations: Protect flowering and early fruit stages with fungicide; post-harvest hot-water dips reduce storage rot on already-harvested fruit.

Citrus___Canker.description: Raised, corky, brown lesions with a yellow halo on leaves, stems, and fruit rind.
Citrus___Canker.organic_treatment: Copper-based bactericide sprays before and after monsoon flush growth; prune and destroy infected twigs.
Citrus___Canker.chemical_treatment: Copper oxychloride or Copper hydroxide sprays timed with new flush growth.
Citrus___Canker.dosage_guidance: Copper oxychloride: 3 g/L water, applied before and during new flush growth periods.
prevention_tips: Control citrus leaf miner (entry wounds worsen canker)
Use windbreaks to reduce bacterial spread
Citrus___Canker.recovery_recommendations: Existing lesions do not heal, but new copper-protected flush growth should emerge clean; prune out heavily infected twigs to reduce inoculum.

Papaya___Ring_spot_virus.causal_agent: Papaya ring spot virus, transmitted by aphids
Papaya___Ring_spot_virus.description: Water-soaked ring/mosaic patterns on fruit, mottled and distorted leaves ('shoestring' leaf symptom), and stunted plant growth.
Papaya___Ring_spot_virus.organic_treatment: No cure — control aphid vectors with reflective mulches and neem oil sprays; remove infected plants.
Papaya___Ring_spot_virus.chemical_treatment: Control aphid vectors with systemic insecticides such as Imidacloprid; there is no chemical cure for the virus itself.
Papaya___Ring_spot_virus.dosage_guidance: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL: 0.3-0.5 ml/L water targeting aphid vectors. The virus itself cannot be treated.
prevention_tips: Use reflective mulch to repel aphids
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Isolate new plantings from infected orchards
Papaya___Ring_spot_virus.recovery_recommendations: Infected plants do not recover — remove promptly to reduce the source of aphid-transmitted spread to healthy plants.

Okra___Yellow_vein_mosaic_virus.causal_agent: Bhendi yellow vein mosaic virus, transmitted by whitefly
Okra___Yellow_vein_mosaic_virus.description: Bright yellow network along leaf veins, stunted growth, and pale, small, deformed fruit.
Okra___Yellow_vein_mosaic_virus.organic_treatment: No cure — manage whitefly vector using yellow sticky traps and neem oil; remove infected plants.
Okra___Yellow_vein_mosaic_virus.chemical_treatment: Control whitefly with Imidacloprid or Thiamethoxam; remove infected plants to reduce virus source.
Okra___Yellow_vein_mosaic_virus.dosage_guidance: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL: 0.3-0.5 ml/L water targeting whitefly vector. No chemical cures the virus directly.
prevention_tips: Avoid planting near infected cotton/okra fields
Okra___Yellow_vein_mosaic_virus.recovery_recommendations: Infected plants remain stunted — remove promptly and focus on vector control for remaining healthy plants.

Cucumber___Powdery_mildew.description: White, powdery fungal patches on the upper and lower leaf surfaces, which can merge to cover the whole leaf and cause premature yellowing.
Cucumber___Powdery_mildew.organic_treatment: Sulfur dust or potassium bicarbonate sprays every 7 days; milk spray (1:9 milk:water) is a common home remedy.
Cucumber___Powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil or Hexaconazole-based fungicide sprays at first sign of white patches.
Cucumber___Powdery_mildew.dosage_guidance: Hexaconazole: 2 ml/L water, repeat every 10 days. Sulfur should not be applied in very hot weather (leaf scorch risk).
prevention_tips: Water at the base, not on leaves
Cucumber___Powdery_mildew.recovery_recommendations: New leaves typically emerge clean once fungicide/sulfur program controls active infection; remove heavily coated leaves to reduce spore load.

Wheat___Yellow_rust.description: Yellow-orange powdery pustules arranged in stripes along leaf veins, most visible in cool, humid weather.
Wheat___Yellow_rust.organic_treatment: Limited organic options — prioritize resistant varieties and early planting to avoid peak disease pressure.
Wheat___Yellow_rust.chemical_treatment: Propiconazole or Tebuconazole-based fungicide at first sighting, repeat after 15-20 days if pressure continues.
Wheat___Yellow_rust.dosage_guidance: Propiconazole: 1 ml/L water, at first pustule sighting, repeat after 15-20 days if disease pressure continues.
prevention_tips: Avoid very early or very late sowing in high-risk zones
Monitor fields weekly during cool weather
Wheat___Yellow_rust.recovery_recommendations: Early fungicide application before rust spreads to the flag leaf is critical for protecting grain yield.

Soybean___Rust.description: Small tan-to-reddish-brown pustules primarily on the leaf underside, causing premature yellowing and defoliation.
Soybean___Rust.organic_treatment: Limited organic options; timely harvest and resistant varieties are the main non-chemical defenses.
Soybean___Rust.chemical_treatment: Azoxystrobin or Tebuconazole-based fungicide at first sign, especially during pod-fill stage.
Soybean___Rust.dosage_guidance: Tebuconazole: 1 ml/L water, applied preventatively at early pod stage in high-risk seasons.
prevention_tips: Plant early to avoid peak rust season
Scout undersides of lower leaves regularly
Avoid dense canopy through proper spacing
Rotate fungicide chemistry to avoid resistance
Soybean___Rust.recovery_recommendations: Fungicide must be applied before significant defoliation to protect pod-fill and yield; heavily defoliated plants will not recover leaf area this season.

Turmeric___Leaf_spot.description: Oval to irregular brown spots with yellow margins scattered across leaves, reducing photosynthetic area and rhizome yield.
Turmeric___Leaf_spot.organic_treatment: Neem cake soil amendment and neem oil foliar sprays; remove and destroy severely spotted leaves.
Turmeric___Leaf_spot.chemical_treatment: Mancozeb or Carbendazim-based sprays every 15 days during the monsoon season.
Turmeric___Leaf_spot.dosage_guidance: Mancozeb: 2-2.5 g/L water, every 15 days during the rainy season.
Turmeric___Leaf_spot.recovery_recommendations: New leaves emerge cleaner once fungicide schedule controls active spread; maintain the program through peak monsoon.

Deficiency___Nitrogen.causal_agent: Insufficient available nitrogen in the soil
Deficiency___Nitrogen.description: Uniform yellowing (chlorosis) starting on older, lower leaves first, with stunted overall growth and thin stems.
Deficiency___Nitrogen.organic_treatment: Apply well-rotted farmyard manure, vermicompost, or a nitrogen-fixing green manure crop in rotation.
Deficiency___Nitrogen.chemical_treatment: Apply Urea or Ammonium Sulfate in split doses matched to the crop's growth stage.
Deficiency___Nitrogen.dosage_guidance: Urea: 40-60 kg/ha in 2-3 split applications, adjusted to crop and soil test results. Not applicable to pesticide dosing — this is a fertility issue, not a pest/disease.
prevention_tips: Use split nitrogen applications rather than one large dose
Deficiency___Nitrogen.recovery_recommendations: New leaves typically green up within 1-2 weeks of correcting nitrogen supply; older yellowed leaves will not fully recover.

Deficiency___Phosphorus.causal_agent: Insufficient available phosphorus in the soil
Deficiency___Phosphorus.description: Dark green or purplish leaf discoloration (especially on undersides and stems), stunted root development, and delayed maturity.
Deficiency___Phosphorus.organic_treatment: Apply bone meal, rock phosphate, or well-composted manure; mycorrhizal inoculants can improve phosphorus uptake.
Deficiency___Phosphorus.chemical_treatment: Apply Single Super Phosphate (SSP) or DAP as a basal dose at sowing/transplanting.
Deficiency___Phosphorus.dosage_guidance: SSP: 50-80 kg/ha as a basal application at sowing. This is a fertility correction, not a pesticide treatment.
prevention_tips: Apply phosphorus as a basal dose before sowing (it moves poorly once applied late)
Maintain soil pH near neutral for better availability
Deficiency___Phosphorus.recovery_recommendations: Correcting phosphorus deficiency mainly benefits future growth stages — plan basal applications for the next planting rather than expecting quick reversal.

Deficiency___Potassium.causal_agent: Insufficient available potassium in the soil
Deficiency___Potassium.description: Yellowing and browning (scorching) along leaf margins and tips, starting on older leaves, with weak stems prone to lodging.
Deficiency___Potassium.organic_treatment: Apply wood ash or compost enriched with potassium-rich organic residues (e.g. banana peel compost).
Deficiency___Potassium.chemical_treatment: Apply Muriate of Potash (MOP) in split doses during vegetative and flowering stages.
Deficiency___Potassium.dosage_guidance: MOP: 40-60 kg/ha in split doses at vegetative and flowering stages. This is a fertility correction, not a pesticide treatment.
prevention_tips: Avoid excess irrigation which leaches potassium from sandy soils
Return crop residues to the soil where possible
Deficiency___Potassium.recovery_recommendations: Symptoms typically improve within 1-2 weeks of correcting potassium supply; already-scorched leaf margins will not reverse.

Deficiency___Iron.causal_agent: Insufficient available iron, often due to high soil pH (alkaline soils)
Deficiency___Iron.description: Yellowing between leaf veins while veins themselves stay green (interveinal chlorosis), most visible on new/young leaves.
Deficiency___Iron.organic_treatment: Apply well-composted organic matter to gradually lower soil pH; foliar spray of diluted compost tea can help.
Deficiency___Iron.chemical_treatment: Foliar spray of chelated iron (Fe-EDTA) for fast correction; soil-applied iron sulfate for longer-term supply.
Deficiency___Iron.dosage_guidance: Fe-EDTA foliar spray: 2-3 g/L water, repeated every 10-15 days. This is a micronutrient correction, not a pesticide treatment.
prevention_tips: Test and monitor soil pH (iron becomes unavailable above pH 7.5)
Use acidifying organic amendments where soil is alkaline
Choose iron-efficient varieties in known problem soils
Deficiency___Iron.recovery_recommendations: Foliar iron sprays green up new growth within days; underlying soil pH should be addressed for a lasting fix.

Deficiency___Zinc.causal_agent: Insufficient available zinc, common in high-pH and heavily-cropped soils
Deficiency___Zinc.description: Small, narrow leaves with interveinal yellowing/bronzing, shortened internodes giving a rosette appearance, and delayed maturity.
Deficiency___Zinc.organic_treatment: Apply well-composted organic manure regularly, which slowly replenishes micronutrient reserves.
Deficiency___Zinc.chemical_treatment: Soil application of Zinc Sulfate at sowing, or a foliar Zinc Sulfate spray for a faster response.
Deficiency___Zinc.dosage_guidance: Zinc sulfate soil application: 20-25 kg/ha at sowing. Foliar spray: 2-5 g/L water. Micronutrient correction, not a pesticide treatment.
prevention_tips: Soil test for zinc every 2-3 years in intensively cropped fields
Avoid excess phosphorus application (can worsen zinc deficiency)
Apply zinc sulfate as a basal dose in known deficient soils
Rotate crops to reduce continuous nutrient mining
Deficiency___Zinc.recovery_recommendations: Foliar zinc sprays typically show visible improvement in new leaves within 1-2 weeks.

Deficiency___Calcium.causal_agent: Insufficient calcium uptake, often due to irregular watering rather than lack of soil calcium
Deficiency___Calcium.description: Dark, sunken, leathery patches at the blossom end of fruit (common in tomato, pepper, watermelon); leaves may show marginal browning in severe cases.
Deficiency___Calcium.organic_treatment: Maintain even soil moisture with mulching; apply gypsum or crushed eggshell compost to soil.
Deficiency___Calcium.chemical_treatment: Foliar calcium chloride or calcium nitrate spray for a faster response, alongside consistent irrigation.
Deficiency___Calcium.dosage_guidance: Calcium chloride foliar spray: 2-4 g/L water, every 7-10 days during fruit development. Consistent watering matters more than calcium supply in most cases.
prevention_tips: Maintain consistent, even soil moisture (mulch helps)
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen or potassium, which can compete with calcium uptake
Test soil calcium levels if the problem persists after irrigation is corrected
Deficiency___Calcium.recovery_recommendations: Already-affected fruit will not recover, but maintaining even watering typically prevents the problem on new fruit within one growth cycle.

Pest___Aphids.description: Small, soft-bodied insects (green, black, or gray) clustering on new growth and leaf undersides, causing curling, yellowing, and sticky honeydew that promotes sooty mold; also spreads viral diseases.
Pest___Aphids.organic_treatment: Spray neem oil (5ml/L) or insecticidal soap every 5-7 days; encourage natural predators like ladybirds.
Pest___Aphids.chemical_treatment: Imidacloprid or Thiamethoxam systemic insecticide if infestation is heavy and honeydew/sooty mold is visible.
Pest___Aphids.dosage_guidance: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL: 0.3-0.5 ml/L water. Neem oil: 5 ml/L with a mild soap emulsifier, every 5-7 days.
prevention_tips: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization (promotes soft, aphid-attractive growth)
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor populations
Pest___Aphids.recovery_recommendations: Plants typically recover new growth within a week once aphid populations are controlled; wash off honeydew/sooty mold with a mild soap spray.

Pest___Whitefly.causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci and related whitefly species
Pest___Whitefly.description: Tiny white flying insects on leaf undersides that suck sap, cause yellowing, sticky honeydew and sooty mold, and are the primary vector for several viral diseases.
Pest___Whitefly.organic_treatment: Yellow sticky traps, neem oil sprays every 5-7 days, and reflective mulches to repel adults.
Pest___Whitefly.chemical_treatment: Imidacloprid, Thiamethoxam, or Spiromesifen systemic insecticide, rotating chemistry to avoid resistance.
Pest___Whitefly.dosage_guidance: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL: 0.3-0.5 ml/L water, every 10 days, rotating with a different chemistry class to slow resistance.
prevention_tips: Use yellow sticky traps for early detection
Remove and destroy heavily infested leaves
Avoid planting susceptible crops next to infested fields
Pest___Whitefly.recovery_recommendations: Controlling whitefly quickly is important not just for direct damage but to prevent viral disease spread; new growth should be clean within 1-2 weeks of control.

Pest___Armyworm.description: Characteristic 'window-pane' feeding damage on young leaves and frass (droppings) inside the whorl; larvae feed deep in the leaf whorl, making them hard to reach with sprays, and can strip a field rapidly.
Pest___Armyworm.organic_treatment: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray applied directly into the leaf whorl; neem seed kernel extract as a repellent.
Pest___Armyworm.chemical_treatment: Spinetoram, Emamectin benzoate, or Chlorantraniliprole insecticide applied directly into the whorl, targeting young larvae before they burrow deeper.
Pest___Armyworm.dosage_guidance: Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC: 0.3 ml/L water, directed into the leaf whorl. Repeat if fresh frass appears after 7-10 days.
prevention_tips: Scout the whorl of young plants weekly from emergence
Use pheromone traps to monitor moth flights
Intercrop with legumes to support natural enemies
Avoid late/staggered planting which extends pest exposure window
Pest___Armyworm.recovery_recommendations: Plants can recover from whorl damage if the growing point survives — targeted whorl application while larvae are small (under 1cm) is far more effective than spraying once larvae are large.

Pest___Brown_planthopper.description: Small brown sap-sucking insects clustering at the base of rice tillers, causing 'hopper burn' — sudden yellowing and drying of patches in the field.
Pest___Brown_planthopper.organic_treatment: Drain field periodically to disrupt breeding; encourage natural predators (spiders, mirid bugs) by reducing broad-spectrum insecticide use.
Pest___Brown_planthopper.chemical_treatment: Imidacloprid or Pymetrozine-based insecticide directed at the base of plants where hoppers cluster.
Pest___Brown_planthopper.dosage_guidance: Pymetrozine 50% WG: 0.3 g/L water, directed at the base of tillers. Avoid repeated use of the same chemical class to prevent resistance (a known issue with this pest).
prevention_tips: Avoid excess nitrogen (promotes dense susceptible canopy)
Use resistant rice varieties where available
Alternate wetting and drying irrigation to disrupt breeding
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide sprays that kill natural predators
Pest___Brown_planthopper.recovery_recommendations: 'Hopper burn' patches usually do not recover — focus treatment on surrounding still-green areas to prevent the patch from expanding.

Pest___Stem_borer.description: Larvae bore into stems, causing a characteristic 'dead heart' (dead central shoot) in vegetative stage or 'whitehead' (empty panicle) at reproductive stage.
Pest___Stem_borer.organic_treatment: Release Trichogramma parasitic wasps as biocontrol; remove and destroy egg masses on leaves.
Pest___Stem_borer.chemical_treatment: Chlorantraniliprole or Cartap hydrochloride granules/spray targeting young larvae before they enter the stem.
Pest___Stem_borer.dosage_guidance: Chlorantraniliprole 0.4% GR: 10 kg/ha broadcast, or 18.5% SC at 0.3 ml/L water as a spray before larvae bore into stems.
prevention_tips: Remove and destroy stubble after harvest (removes overwintering larvae)
Use pheromone traps to monitor moth activity
Avoid staggered planting dates in the same area
Pest___Stem_borer.recovery_recommendations: Once larvae are inside the stem, sprays are far less effective — dead hearts/whiteheads will not recover; prevention and early-stage treatment are key.

Pest___Pink_bollworm.description: Larvae bore into cotton bolls and feed on seeds, causing rosette flowers, damaged locules, and stained lint that reduces quality and yield.
Pest___Pink_bollworm.organic_treatment: Pheromone mating-disruption traps; destroy crop residue and unopened bolls after harvest to break the pest cycle.
Pest___Pink_bollworm.chemical_treatment: Emamectin benzoate or Chlorantraniliprole insecticide at first sign of rosette flowers, before larvae enter bolls.
Pest___Pink_bollworm.dosage_guidance: Emamectin benzoate 5% SG: 0.4 g/L water, applied at first rosette flower sighting — timing before boll entry is critical.
prevention_tips: Destroy crop residue and unopened bolls immediately after final harvest
Use pheromone traps for early detection and mating disruption
Avoid extending the growing season unnecessarily
Rotate to non-host crops where pink bollworm pressure is high
Pest___Pink_bollworm.recovery_recommendations: Once larvae are inside bolls, control is very difficult — prevention via residue destruction and early-season monitoring is far more effective than in-boll treatment.

Pest___Fruit_and_shoot_borer.description: Larvae bore into shoots causing wilting of terminal shoots ('dead heart'), and later bore into fruit, leaving entry holes plugged with frass.
Pest___Fruit_and_shoot_borer.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy wilted shoots and infested fruit weekly; pheromone traps for monitoring and mass trapping.
Pest___Fruit_and_shoot_borer.chemical_treatment: Chlorantraniliprole or Spinosad insecticide at first sign of shoot wilting, before larvae move to fruit.
Pest___Fruit_and_shoot_borer.dosage_guidance: Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC: 0.3 ml/L water, at first wilted shoot sighting, repeat every 10-14 days during fruiting.
prevention_tips: Remove and destroy wilted shoots and infested fruit weekly (do not compost)
Use pheromone traps for mass trapping
Avoid continuous brinjal/okra cropping in the same field
Pest___Fruit_and_shoot_borer.recovery_recommendations: Plants regrow new shoots once infested tips are removed; consistent weekly removal of infested plant parts is as important as spraying.

Pest___Diamondback_moth.description: Small green caterpillars create irregular 'window pane' holes in leaves, feeding mostly on the underside, and can cause severe defoliation on young plants.
Pest___Diamondback_moth.organic_treatment: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray targeting young larvae; encourage parasitic wasps by reducing broad-spectrum sprays.
Pest___Diamondback_moth.chemical_treatment: Spinosad or Emamectin benzoate insecticide, rotating chemistry each generation to manage this pest's well-known resistance tendency.
Pest___Diamondback_moth.dosage_guidance: Spinosad 45% SC: 0.3 ml/L water. Emamectin benzoate 5% SG: 0.4 g/L water. Rotate chemistries each spray cycle — this pest develops resistance quickly.
prevention_tips: Rotate insecticide chemistry classes strictly (high resistance risk)
Use pheromone traps to monitor moth activity
Intercrop with trap crops like mustard
Pest___Diamondback_moth.recovery_recommendations: Young plants can recover from moderate leaf damage; treat early since heavily defoliated seedlings may not form marketable heads.

Pest___Pod_borer.description: Larvae bore round holes into pods and feed on developing seeds, often with the head end inside the pod and body hanging out while feeding.
Pest___Pod_borer.organic_treatment: HaNPV (nucleopolyhedrovirus) biopesticide spray targeting young larvae; encourage bird perches to increase predation.
Pest___Pod_borer.chemical_treatment: Emamectin benzoate or Chlorantraniliprole insecticide at first sign of pod damage, targeting young larvae.
Pest___Pod_borer.dosage_guidance: Emamectin benzoate 5% SG: 0.4 g/L water, applied at first pod damage sighting, repeat after 10-14 days if pressure continues.
prevention_tips: Use pheromone traps for early moth detection
Install bird perches to boost natural predation
Intercrop with sorghum/maize as a trap-crop border
Avoid continuous pulse cropping in the same field
Pest___Pod_borer.recovery_recommendations: Undamaged pods on the same plant continue to develop normally; focus treatment on protecting remaining pods rather than damaged ones.

Pest___Thrips.description: Tiny slender insects that rasp and suck plant tissue, causing silvery streaks, leaf curling, and stippling, especially on new growth and flowers.
Pest___Thrips.organic_treatment: Blue sticky traps for monitoring, neem oil sprays every 5-7 days, and encouraging predatory mites.
Pest___Thrips.chemical_treatment: Fipronil or Spinosad-based insecticide, rotating chemistry to slow resistance development.
Pest___Thrips.dosage_guidance: Fipronil 5% SC: 1-1.5 ml/L water, every 10 days. Spinosad 45% SC: 0.3 ml/L water as an alternate rotation.
prevention_tips: Use blue sticky traps for early monitoring
Remove and destroy weeds that host thrips between crops
Avoid moisture stress which increases thrips susceptibility
Rotate insecticide classes to manage resistance
Pest___Thrips.recovery_recommendations: New growth typically emerges normal once thrips populations are reduced; already-silvered/curled leaves will not fully recover their appearance.

Pest___Mealybug.description: White, waxy, cottony masses clustering on stems, leaf axils, and roots; secretes honeydew leading to sooty mold, and weakens plants over time.
Pest___Mealybug.organic_treatment: Wipe off colonies with alcohol-dipped cotton for small infestations; neem oil or insecticidal soap sprays every 5-7 days.
Pest___Mealybug.chemical_treatment: Imidacloprid or Buprofezin systemic insecticide as a soil drench or foliar spray for larger infestations.
Pest___Mealybug.dosage_guidance: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL: 0.3-0.5 ml/L water as foliar spray or soil drench, every 10-15 days.
prevention_tips: Inspect new plants before introducing them near existing crops
Control ants (they protect mealybugs from predators for honeydew)
Prune and destroy heavily infested plant parts
Pest___Mealybug.recovery_recommendations: Wash off honeydew/sooty mold with mild soapy water after treatment; plants typically resume normal growth within 1-2 weeks of control.

Pest___Red_spider_mite.causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae and related mite species
Pest___Red_spider_mite.description: Tiny reddish mites (not insects) causing fine stippling/bronzing on leaves and delicate webbing on the underside, especially in hot, dry conditions.
Pest___Red_spider_mite.organic_treatment: Spray plain water to dislodge mites; neem oil or sulfur-based miticide sprays every 5-7 days.
Pest___Red_spider_mite.chemical_treatment: Abamectin, Spiromesifen, or Fenpyroximate miticide (not a general insecticide — regular insecticides are largely ineffective against mites).
Pest___Red_spider_mite.dosage_guidance: Abamectin 1.8% EC: 0.5 ml/L water, every 7-10 days. True miticides are required — standard insecticides do not control mites well.
prevention_tips: Avoid drought stress (mites thrive in hot, dry conditions)
Increase humidity around plants where practical
Avoid excess nitrogen (promotes lush, mite-attractive growth)
Rotate miticide chemistry to manage resistance
Pest___Red_spider_mite.recovery_recommendations: Improving irrigation to reduce plant stress alongside miticide treatment speeds recovery; heavily stippled leaves will not fully green up but new growth should be clean.

Pest___Jassid.causal_agent: Amrasca biguttula and related leafhopper species
Pest___Jassid.description: Small wedge-shaped green insects that suck sap from the underside of leaves, causing yellowing, downward curling, and a characteristic bronze/reddish 'hopper burn' on leaf margins (common on cotton and okra).
Pest___Jassid.organic_treatment: Neem oil sprays every 5-7 days; yellow sticky traps for monitoring populations.
Pest___Jassid.chemical_treatment: Imidacloprid or Acetamiprid systemic insecticide at first sign of leaf curling/yellowing.
Pest___Jassid.dosage_guidance: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL: 0.3-0.5 ml/L water, every 10 days during peak activity periods.
prevention_tips: Encourage natural predators by minimizing broad-spectrum sprays
Pest___Jassid.recovery_recommendations: New leaves typically emerge normal once populations are controlled; curled and bronzed leaves will not reverse but do not usually need removal.

Pest___Fruit_fly.description: Adult flies lay eggs inside ripening fruit; maggots feed internally causing rot, premature fruit drop, and visible entry-point punctures on the skin.
Pest___Fruit_fly.organic_treatment: Methyl eugenol or protein-bait traps for mass trapping of male flies; collect and destroy fallen/infested fruit daily.
Pest___Fruit_fly.chemical_treatment: Spinosad-based bait spray applied to fruit surface (not systemic) to attract and kill adult flies before egg-laying.
Pest___Fruit_fly.dosage_guidance: Spinosad bait spray applied as per label to fruit surface/foliage in spots, not a full-cover spray — bait formulations work by attraction, not full coverage.
prevention_tips: Collect and destroy fallen and infested fruit daily (breaks the breeding cycle)
Use methyl eugenol traps for mass trapping of males
Bag developing fruit with paper/net bags where feasible
Deep-till soil after harvest to expose pupae to predators/heat
Pest___Fruit_fly.recovery_recommendations: Already-infested fruit cannot be saved — focus on protecting the remaining unripe fruit through trapping and sanitation for the rest of the season.

Healthy.description: No signs of disease, pest damage, or nutrient deficiency were detected. Leaf color and texture appear normal.
Healthy.organic_treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular monitoring and good agronomic practices.
Healthy.recovery_recommendations: No action needed — plant appears healthy.
